29.7%

Fatigue - Preoperative / Bariatric Clearance · 48M, BMI 43, fatigue before bariatric clearance · 2026-08-01 | **Score:** 29.69% (Avg 61.8%) | **Patient:** 48M, BMI 43, fatigue before bariatric clearance

First Principles · Brilliant Attending

Picture the upper airway as a floppy hose held open by muscle tone while awake.

At sleep onset, pharyngeal dilators quiet. In BMI 43, fat pads in the lateral pharyngeal walls and tongue base already narrow the lumen. When tone drops, the walls approximate. Airflow stops. Oxygen falls. CO2 rises. The brain briefly arouses, tone returns, the airway pops open with a snort, and sleep fragments. Repeat hundreds of times. Morning arrives after nine hours in bed with almost no consolidated restorative sleep. That is daytime hypersomnolence with a "normal" sleep duration.

Spatial logic. Pathology is nocturnal and oropharyngeal. Daytime lung and heart exams can be clean. A normal CBC hematocrit does not rule it out. Facial bone films and an ENT shrug do not open a collapsed airway. Mild pulmonary hypertension on echo is a whisper of chronic intermittent hypoxia, not the diagnosis.

Contrast — central vs obstructive. Central apnea is the brainstem forgetting to breathe. Obstructive apnea is the pipe collapsing while the drive to breathe is still there. Obesity points hard at obstruction. Polysomnography separates them.

Connecting thread — bariatric clearance. Anesthesia relaxes the same dilators. Untreated OSA means a difficult airway, postop desaturation, and cardiopulmonary risk. The case ends when you order CPAP after a positive sleep study. Insulin and a calorie-restricted diet matter for surgical readiness, but they are not the OSA treatment.

Case 141
Phenylketonuria (PKU) — Newborn — Attending Walkthrough
15.9%

Rash - Pediatrics · 3-week-old female, 3.4 kg, irritability, eczema, musty-smelling diaper · 2026-07-28 | **Score:** 15.87% (Avg 38.5%) | **Patient:** 3-week-old female, 3.4 kg, irritability, eczema, musty-smelling diaper

First Principles · Brilliant Attending

Picture phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH) sitting in the liver. It takes phenylalanine — an essential amino acid from dietary protein — and adds a hydroxyl group to the benzene ring, converting it to tyrosine. This reaction needs tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) as a cofactor and molecular oxygen. It is the only way out for phenylalanine. There is no backup pathway.

In classic PKU, the PAH gene on chromosome 12 has a mutation — usually a missense mutation that reduces enzyme activity to less than 1% of normal. Phenylalanine arrives from the diet and cannot leave. It accumulates. Serum levels climb from normal (<2 mg/dL) to 20+ mg/dL.

Three things happen with that accumulation:

1. Brain toxicity. Phenylalanine competes with other large neutral amino acids (tyrosine, tryptophan) for the LAT1 transporter at the blood-brain barrier. High phenylalanine outcompetes them. The brain becomes starved of tyrosine (needed for dopamine, norepinephrine, epinephrine synthesis) and tryptophan (needed for serotonin). Myelination fails. White matter lesions form. IQ drops — irreversible if untreated in the first weeks of life. Every day of delay costs measurable IQ points.

2. Melanin deficiency. Tyrosine is the precursor for melanin. When PAH is blocked, tyrosine production falls. Melanocytes in skin, hair, and iris cannot make pigment. Untreated PKU children develop fair skin, blonde hair, and blue eyes — regardless of genetic background. This patient is only 3 weeks old, so not enough time has passed for this manifestation. But it is coming.

3. Musty odor. Phenylalanine accumulates to the point where alternative metabolic pathways kick in. Phenylalanine transaminase converts it to phenylpyruvic acid, which decarboxylates to phenylacetic acid. Phenylacetic acid is volatile. It is excreted in sweat and urine. It smells musty, mousy — the pathognomonic odor of PKU. The mother notices it in the diaper. That one observation is worth more than the entire meningitis workup you ordered.

The clinical anchor: A newborn with irritability, eczema, and musty-smelling urine = PKU until proven otherwise. One blood test. One dietary change.

✕

▾
Phenylalanine, serum
First principles

PAH deficiency blocks phenylalanine → tyrosine. Serum phenylalanine >20 mg/dL confirms PKU. This one lab scores 45% of your grade. You ordered 14 orders — not one of them was the right one. Diagnosis: 13.04%.

Diet, low protein / Nutrition consult
First principles

PKU treatment is dietary phenylalanine restriction for life. Special low-phenylalanine formula + measured breast milk. Without it: irreversible intellectual disability. Treatment: 0%.

✓
What I Got Right
▾

You examined the skin (eczema is a PKU manifestation — phenylalanine crystals in sweat irritate the skin). You investigated the strange-smelling diaper. You recognized the infant was sick and needed workup. You sequenced correctly and stayed in the right location. The problem was not effort or thoroughness. It was pattern recognition. You saw "sick newborn" and went straight to sepsis/meningitis — which is the right reflex in a febrile neonate. But this infant was afebrile (36.1 C). She had eczema. She had a strange smell. The pattern was metabolic, not infectious.

⚠
What I Got Wrong - Wrong Orders4 items
▾
LP + CSF studies (bacterial, fungal, viral, cryptococcal, AFB, cytology)
Why this order failed

Picture a 3-week-old with meningitis. She is febrile, lethargic, feeding poorly, fontanelle bulging. This infant was 36.1 C, irritable with eczema, and a musty diaper. No fever. No meningismus. The smell and the skin are metabolic fingerprints, not CSF fingerprints. LP was a fishing expedition in the wrong ocean. Invasive workups feel thorough. Thoroughness in the wrong direction still scores near zero on diagnosis.

Galactokinase, blood
Why this order failed

Galactokinase deficiency lives in the galactose pathway (cataracts, galactosuria). It does not dump phenylalanine into sweat, does not make musty odor, and does not cause this eczema pattern. You reached for "metabolic newborn" but grabbed the wrong enzyme. Smell + eczema points to PAH/PKU, not the galactose trap.

CBC, BMP, UA (screening labs)
Why this order failed

These are never "wrong" in a sick child. They also never diagnose PKU. UA ketones use nitroprusside for acetoacetate / beta-hydroxybutyrate. Phenylacetic acid does not light that up, so UA can look "ketones negative" while the infant is drowning in phenylalanine. The name phenylketonuria is a historical trap. Diagnosis is serum phenylalanine, not urine.

Timing: negative patient update before treatment
Why this order failed

Timing scored 0%. You advanced the clock / took a hit before the correct treatment existed. In PKU every delay is myelination damage. Even if the invasive orders were "allowed," the clock without diet is the real injury.

Bottom line: 14 orders, 0 of them were serum phenylalanine or low-protein diet / nutrition consult. The miss list is short. The wrong-direction list is long.

Osteoporosis — Postmenopausal, Foot Fracture from Tripping
15.3%

Foot Pain - Internal Medicine · Postmenopausal woman · Foot pain after tripping · Fracture from minimal trauma · 2026-07-27 | **Score:** 15.3% (Avg 62.3%) | **Diagnosis:** Osteoporosis

First Principles · Brilliant Attending

The Osteoporosis Cascade

  1. Estrogen withdrawal at menopause. Estrogen suppresses osteoclast activity through RANKL/OPG signaling. When estrogen drops, RANKL rises. Osteoclasts go unchecked. Bone resorption outpaces bone formation. This is why postmenopausal women lose 2-3% of bone mass per year for the first 5-7 years after menopause.
  1. Trabecular bone goes first. Osteoporosis hits trabecular (spongy) bone before cortical bone. Trabecular bone has higher surface area and turnover rate. The vertebrae, femoral neck, and distal radius are trabecular-rich and fracture first. The metatarsals also have significant trabecular content — a foot fracture from tripping is a sentinel event.
  1. Vitamin D deficiency accelerates the loss. Vitamin D is needed for intestinal calcium absorption. Without it, only 10-15% of dietary calcium is absorbed. The parathyroid glands sense the low serum calcium and secrete PTH. PTH pulls calcium from bone. Chronic secondary hyperparathyroidism from vitamin D deficiency is a silent bone thief that operates alongside postmenopausal osteoporosis.
  1. The fragility fracture is a predictor, not an endpoint. A woman who fractures her metatarsal from tripping has the same bone pathology as the woman who will fracture her hip next year. The foot fracture is the warning. DEXA confirms the T-score. Treatment prevents the hip fracture.

The Diagnostic Algorithm

StepOrderWhy
1Foot X-ray (not ankle)Ankle X-ray does not reliably visualize metatarsals. You ordered ankle. This was the wrong study.
2Bone densitometry (DEXA)Quantifies bone mineral density. T-score ≤ -2.5 = osteoporosis. This is the screening test.
3Vitamin D 25-OHLow vitamin D worsens osteoporosis and must be repleted before or with bisphosphonates.
4CBC + CMPCBC: rule out multiple myeloma (anemia, rouleaux). CMP: calcium, alkaline phosphatase, renal function. You did these — correct.

The Treatment Ladder

StepOrderWhy
1Vitamin D supplementationReplete deficiency. 800-2000 IU/day.
2Oral bisphosphonate (alendronate 70 mg weekly, first-line)Binds hydroxyapatite in bone. Taken up by osteoclasts during resorption. Induces osteoclast apoptosis. Net effect: reduced bone resorption. Reduces vertebral fracture risk by 40-50%, hip fracture by 30-40%.
3Exercise counselingWeight-bearing exercise stimulates osteoblast activity through mechanical loading (Wolff's law).
✓
What I Got Right
▾
Physical exam triage — general appearance + extremities/spine. Correct approach.
  • CBC with differential — ruled out multiple myeloma and other marrow disorders
  • CMP — checked calcium, renal function, alkaline phosphatase
  • Correctly avoided — raloxifene (no breast cancer indication), estrogen-progestin (contraindicated — increased breast cancer, stroke, clotting risk)
  • No inappropriate invasive orders
  • Correct sequencing

Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome — Attending Walkthrough
14.8%

Chronic Diarrhea - Internal Medicine · 45M music teacher, 3 years of diarrhea · 2026-07-27 | **Score:** 14.77% (Avg 41.3%) | **Patient:** 45M music teacher, 3 years of diarrhea

First Principles · Brilliant Attending

The physics of acid diarrhea

Picture the gastric parietal cell. On its apical membrane sits the H+/K+-ATPase -- the proton pump. This pump exchanges intracellular H+ for luminal K+, pumping HCl into the stomach lumen at a concentration gradient of 1,000,000:1. One million times more acidic than blood.

Normally, gastrin -- released from G cells in the gastric antrum -- nudges that pump. A little gastrin → a little acid. Food comes in, gastrin goes up, acid goes up, food is digested, gastrin goes down, acid goes down. Beautiful feedback control.

A gastrinoma breaks that feedback loop. The tumor cells secrete gastrin autonomously -- no food trigger needed, no negative feedback from low gastric pH. The result is a parietal cell bombardment: gastrin binds CCK-B receptors on every parietal cell, activates adenylate cyclase → cAMP → PKA → phosphorylation of the proton pump → massive, unregulated HCl secretion.

Why this causes diarrhea -- two mechanisms, one source

Mechanism 1: Secretory diarrhea. Normal small intestine absorbs water by absorbing sodium. Sodium absorption requires a neutral pH environment. When the gastric effluent is pure acid, the duodenal and jejunal mucosa cannot absorb sodium. Water follows sodium -- but sodium isn't going anywhere, so water stays in the lumen. High-volume watery diarrhea.

Mechanism 2: Malabsorptive diarrhea. Pancreatic lipase has a pH optimum of ~7-8. When the duodenal pH drops to 2-3 from the acid flood, lipase is irreversibly inactivated. No lipase = no fat digestion. Meanwhile, bile salts -- which need to be deprotonated to form micelles -- precipitate at low pH. No micelles = no fat absorption. The result: undigested fat passes through, producing the foul-smelling, oily, greasy stools characteristic of steatorrhea.

Two mechanisms, one root cause. The acid is the beginning, the middle, and the end of this story.

The heartburn tells you the diagnosis

This patient said his heartburn "improved when he was given pantoprazole." That's the smoking gun. A PPI directly and irreversibly blocks the H+/K+-ATPase. It doesn't matter how much gastrin is screaming -- if the proton pump is inhibited, acid doesn't form. The fact that PPI worked proves the symptoms are acid-mediated.

The differential for acid hypersecretion includes:

  • Zollinger-Ellison (gastrinoma) -- autonomous gastrin, very high acid output
  • Antral G-cell hyperplasia -- too many gastrin-producing cells
  • Retained gastric antrum -- post-Billroth II surgery complication
  • H. pylori -- stimulates gastrin (but more commonly causes ulcers)

The history of chronic diarrhea + steatorrhea + PPI-responsive heartburn + negative sigmoidoscopy = the problem is in the foregut, not the hindgut.

What You Got Right

Your physical exam was solid: general appearance, cardiac, abdomen, rectal. Stool occult blood negative (not a bleeding ulcer -- consistent with ZES acid damage that hasn't penetrated to vessels yet). CBC and CMP were appropriate screening. ESR and CRP negative (no inflammatory process). Magnesium and phosphorus normal.

The upper GI / small bowel X-ray was an optional order -- not required but it would have been abnormal if done.

What You Missed

MissedImpact
Serum gastrinThe diagnostic test. Gastrin >1,000 pg/mL (10x upper normal limit) is diagnostic of ZES. This patient: 1,200. Ordering this one lab would have changed everything.
Upper GI endoscopyLocates the gastrinoma. Nodule in duodenal wall → biopsy shows benign gastric metaplasia. This is definitive structural diagnosis.
CT abdomen/pelvisStaging. Gastrinomas can be malignant and metastasize to liver (40% of duodenal gastrinomas). Must check before planning surgery.
PPI (omeprazole/pantoprazole)The treatment for acid hypersecretion. PPI blocks the H+/K+-ATPase directly -- the final common pathway -- regardless of how much gastrin is upstream. Without acid control: ongoing ulcer risk, continued diarrhea, progressive esophagitis.
Surgical consultSporadic gastrinomas are surgically curable. This is not a medical management case for life -- it's a surgical case if the tumor is resectable.
Pre-op labs (PT/PTT, type & screen, ECG)Patient is heading to surgery. Bleeding risk, blood availability, cardiac clearance.
MEN1 screening (PTH, ionized Ca, prolactin)25% of ZES cases are associated with Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia Type 1. If MEN1 is present, the surgical approach changes: multifocal disease, harder to cure surgically, more often managed medically. Screen BEFORE surgery -- always.
Smoking cessationCigars 2x/week. Smoking worsens peptic ulcer disease and delays healing. Every visit is preventive medicine.

Location Error

You kept the patient in the office. ZES with a resectable gastrinoma requires admission to the inpatient unit for surgical intervention. At simulated time Day 2 + 10:20, the correct location was Inpatient Unit. You were still in Office.

13.8%

Depression - Internal Medicine · 42F, "depression" that is cortisol · 2026-07-29 | **Score:** 13.75% (Avg 68.3%) | **Patient:** 42F, "depression" that is cortisol

First Principles · Brilliant Attending

A corticotroph microadenoma in the pituitary dumps ACTH. Both adrenals answer. Cortisol never sleeps. The normal midnight nadir dies. Muscle wastes. Fat moves central. Androgens rise (hirsutism). GnRH axis shuts down (amenorrhea). The brain feels the steroid storm as depression — but SSRIs do not cut ACTH.

Stepwise CCS logic:

  1. Prove hypercortisolism (late-night salivary cortisol, 24h UFC, or low-dose DST)
  2. Measure ACTH (here 166 → ACTH-dependent)
  3. MRI pituitary (microadenoma; may be MRI-negative → IPSS)
  4. Neurosurgery: transsphenoidal resection

Pregnancy test first when amenorrhea is on the board.

Von Willebrand Disease (Menorrhagia) — Attending Walkthrough
10.0%

14F, heavy menses since menarche, epistaxis, easy bruising, prolonged dental bleed, mother with menorrhagia · 2026-07-28 | **Score:** 10% (Avg 59.6%) | **Patient:** 14F, heavy menses since menarche, epistaxis, easy bruising, prolonged dental bleed, mother with menorrhagia

First Principles · Brilliant Attending

Picture a cut on a high-shear mucosal surface — endometrium, nasal mucosa, gum after extraction. Collagen is exposed. Platelets must stick.

von Willebrand factor is the rope. It binds exposed collagen at one end and platelet GPIb at the other. It also cradles Factor VIII in plasma so FVIII is not cleared. Without enough functional vWF, platelets cannot tether under shear, and FVIII levels fall secondarily. The clotting factor cascade may still look mostly normal on a PT/INR sheet. The primary plug fails first.

That is why the bleeding is mucosal and cutaneous — nose, mouth, uterus, bruises — not deep joint bleeds like severe hemophilia. Hemophilia destroys the fibrin mesh deep in joints and muscle. vWD fails at the sticky first contact on wet, high-flow surfaces.

Menarche is the stress test. Every month the endometrium sheds under arterial shear. Mild type 1 vWD (quantitative deficiency) can hide in childhood, then explode as menorrhagia. The mother's undiagnosed heavy periods are the autosomal dominant fingerprint.

Labs write the same story:

  • CBC: anemia from blood loss, normal platelet count (not ITP)
  • PT normal, aPTT normal or only mildly long, fibrinogen normal
  • Ristocetin-induced platelet aggregation reduced
  • vWF activity assay confirms — but takes ~3 days. You treat before the lab returns.

First principles

First principles

Anemia + normal platelets. Separates vWD from thrombocytopenia. Hgb ~10 — not transfusion territory yet.

PT/PTT
First principles

Places you on the bleeding-disorder table. vWD pattern is normal platelets, normal PT, normal/mild long aPTT.

Platelet aggregation / ristocetin
First principles

Functional clue while waiting on vWF activity.

vWF activity or heme consult
First principles

Confirms type 1. Results late — empiric therapy now.

TSH
First principles

Hypothyroid menorrhagia mimic — rule out.

IV fluids
First principles

Volume bridge. Do not drown her in fluid and dilute the little vWF she has. No pRBCs at Hgb 10 unless she crashes.

DDAVP
First principles

Releases endothelial vWF/FVIII stores. Onset 30–60 min. Empiric for suspected type 1. Avoid if type 2B suspected.

Tranexamic acid
First principles

Blocks plasmin. Protects the clot on mucosal surfaces. Start with DDAVP, not after failure.

No NSAIDs / no contact sports
First principles

NSAIDs cripple the platelets she still has. Soccer = trauma risk.

Iron
First principles

Replace what months of menorrhagia stole.

OCP / GYN
First principles

Estrogen raises vWF/FVIII and calms the endometrium — prevention, not just acute stop.

PTSD — The 1-Month Line That Separates Acute Stress from Trauma Disorder
7.5%

· 2026-07-26

First Principles · Brilliant Attending

The Neurobiology of Trauma Memory

When a knife enters the chest, the amygdala does not file the memory in the hippocampus like a normal autobiographical event. The extreme sympathetic surge — norepinephrine flooding the basolateral amygdala — tags the sensory fragments of the event (the glint of the blade, the smell of the alley, the sound of the attacker's voice) with supraphysiologic emotional salience.

Normally, the prefrontal cortex inhibits the amygdala through top-down GABAergic projections. In the days after trauma, this circuit re-calibrates. For most people, the amygdala quiets, the hippocampus contextualizes the memory as "past," and the prefrontal cortex regains inhibitory control. This is the arc of acute stress: 3 days to 1 month of intrusive symptoms that resolve as the memory is processed.

In PTSD, this re-calibration fails. The prefrontal-amygdala circuit does not recover its inhibitory tone. The hippocampus shrinks (glucocorticoid toxicity from sustained cortisol on CA1 neurons). The amygdala remains hyper-responsive to trauma-associated cues. The result: the memory stays "present tense" — not something that happened, but something that is happening.

The DSM-5 Criterion F — Why 1 Month Matters

DiagnosisDurationThis patient?
Acute Stress Disorder3 days to 1 monthNo — 5 weeks (35 days)
PTSD>1 monthYes

This is not an arbitrary cutoff. It reflects the expected window for natural recovery. If symptoms persist beyond 1 month, the neurobiological failure to extinguish the fear memory is likely permanent without treatment. You cannot "wait and see" at week 5. The brain has already shown you it cannot self-correct.
